paras: The killing of Leroy Mitchell was the shooting of a Black man by a white man near Alton, Halifax County, Virginia, in mid-August 1920, after a posse trailed him on an accusation that he had attempted to attack a white girl. Mitchell died of shotgun wounds, and no arrest had been reported a week later. White papers carried the Associated Press account of a brother avenging his sister, while the Chicago Defender reported that Mitchell had only tipped his hat to the girl.

According to an Associated Press dispatch from Danville dated August 14, Mitchell was accused of attempting to attack a white girl near Alton a few hours before he was shot. The dispatch said a posse trailed and caught him, that he "showed fight with an ax when cornered," and that the girl's brother fired a load from a shotgun into his stomach. Mitchell died, in the AP's words, "shortly after being carried to the Houston jail."

A separately worded Danville dispatch in the Washington Herald named the young woman as Miss Mattie Ramsey of Alton and said her screams "brought help." That account called Mitchell "a South Carolina negro" and said he died at the Halifax County jail of wounds received when he tried to elude "a posse of farmers," without mentioning the brother or an ax.

The Chicago Defender's Danville correspondent reported on August 20 that efforts to learn the shooter's name had failed. Officials told the paper that naming the girl's brother might injure her "good character," and no arrest had been made. No report of an inquest, grand jury or trial was found in the coverage.

The Associated Press item ran from August 14 to 16 in the Chattanooga News, the Union Daily Times of South Carolina, the Richmond Times-Dispatch and the Alexandria Gazette, often cut to its first sentence or two. Headlines such as "Brother Kills Negro Who Attacked Sister" and "Slays Assailant of Sister" stated the alleged attack as fact and cast the shooting as a brother's act. Only the Washington Herald qualified the charge with "it is alleged."

The Chicago Defender, in a front-page item headed "Tips Hat to Girl," gave a different cause, saying Mitchell had tipped his hat to a white girl "whom he had mistaken for a girl of his Race." It put the words "too fresh" and "assault" in quotation marks as the white man's charges and described Mitchell as "well known in this section." The Defender also stressed that officials withheld the shooter's name and that no one had been arrested, points absent from the white coverage.

The accounts differ on the cause, the shooting and the place of death. The white papers reported an attempted attack or assault, while the Defender reported a tipped hat and an accusation of being "too fresh." The claim that Mitchell fought with an ax appears only in the AP dispatch, which the Washington Herald's version of a man shot while trying to elude his pursuers does not repeat. He was said to have died at the Houston jail, at the Halifax County jail, or at a hospital.

reader.title: Killing of Leroy Mitchell
bases: A posse trailed and caught Mitchell after an accusation involving a white girl, and the girl's brother shot him dead; no officer or legal process is reported (A3, A4, A6).

Mitchell was hunted down by a 'posse of farmers' and shot after capture by a private citizen acting on an accusation of attempted assault on a white girl, with no lawful authority reported and no arrest (A3, A4, A6); the posse's size is not given and the AP presents the shot as a response to Mitchell fighting with an ax, an account from the pursuers' side.

The AP dispatch (A3), a separately worded Danville dispatch in the Washington Herald (A4) and the Chicago Defender (A6) agree that Leroy Mitchell was shot dead near Alton, Halifax County, after an accusation concerning a white girl, though they differ on the shooter, the cause and where he died.

accounts.label: Associated Press (Danville)
accounts.gist: Mitchell attempted to attack a white girl near Alton; a posse trailed and caught him, he 'showed fight with an ax' when cornered, and the girl's brother shot him in the stomach; he died after being carried to the Houston jail.

accounts.label: Washington Herald dispatch (Danville)
accounts.gist: Mitchell, 'a South Carolina negro', died at the Halifax County jail of shotgun wounds received while trying to elude a posse of farmers who had trailed him after an alleged attempted assault on Miss Mattie Ramsey.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender correspondent (Danville)
accounts.gist: Mitchell tipped his hat to a white girl he mistook for a Black girl; a white man, her brother, accused him of being 'too fresh' and of attempting to 'assault' her and shot him; he died at a hospital, and no arrest was made.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Slays Assailant of Sister' and 'Brother Kills Negro Who Attacked Sister' state the alleged attack as fact and present the shooting as a brother's response, with the ax detail as the pursuers' justification.
The AP item ran as a brief in Tennessee, South Carolina and Virginia papers, cut to one or two sentences outside Richmond and Alexandria.
Under 'Tips Hat to Girl' the Defender put the alleged assault in quotation marks, attributed the death to a tipped hat, and noted that officials shielded the shooter's name and made no arrest.

info: On or shortly before August 14, 1920 (AP dispatch dated Danville, Aug. 14, reporting news 'reaching here today'); the Washington Herald says he died 'today' under a dateline whose day is illegible.
Near Alton, Halifax County; death at the 'Houston jail' (AP), the 'Halifax County jail' (Washington Herald) or a 'hospital' (Chicago Defender).
Leroy Mitchell, Black; called 'a South Carolina negro' by the Washington Herald and 'well known in this section' by the Chicago Defender.

Accused of attempting to attack (or assault) a white girl, named by the Washington Herald as Miss Mattie Ramsey of Alton; the Chicago Defender says he had tipped his hat to a white girl he mistook for a Black girl and was accused of being 'too fresh'.

The girl's brother (unnamed) fired the shot, according to the AP; the Washington Herald says the wounds came from a 'posse of farmers'; the Defender says 'the white man', whose name officials withheld.
None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
